notes.title: Dev Diary #5: Designing the Train Level
notes.content:
[h3]My name is Sixten. I’m one of the artists working on Ground Zero and I’m here to talk about the art of the train level. [/h3]

So what makes the train level so unique compared to other levels in Ground Zero?

Since the train level is a more cramped space than the areas in other levels, we focused more of our attention on materials and textures. Another key difference compared is that the train is moving, which presented unique challenges.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/f2506c39df1364f5c1972d34d65e3e0ced4c2ff4.png[/img]

In terms of design, the train is mainly inspired by the Orient Express, but with some inspiration from late 1800s architecture. So in short, the train is made up, but we did take inspiration from many different real-world places! We wanted to achieve an “upper class” and old feeling environment! Levels set in claustrophobic trains or on the subway were commonplace in classic survival horror games, so that’s the vibe we were going for. In particular, the train level in Resident Evil 0 was a great source of inspiration!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/76033890fc52073480b3935b0c9577805b751659.png[/img][i]The train level in Resident Evil 0.[/i]

The train is constantly moving, which as you can imagine presents an unique challenge in a prerendered game. Also, since the train is moving quite fast, designing the world around the train would involve a lot of work. To combat these problems, the train isn’t actually moving, rather the world around it is. So we built the environment in chunks that move past the train and will give the illusion of the train moving. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/b211e46a8c1294f0334b4e946c6e8a7fa59a55a5.gif[/img]
[i]The prototype of the world moving outside of the train.[/i]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/5a321bafa403452f6bb60fab985ea0ad90113581.gif[/img]
[i]The finalised view from the train window.[/i]

Another big challenge with creating a level like this is the cramped and linear design you naturally get from a train. There’s not much room to move around and kite enemies, so combat is a lot harder to get right. There’s also less you can do artistically with a restricted and linear space like this. Because of this, we had to make sure that the level wasn't too long, that it feels just right. And that the train feels interesting all the way through! 

There are a lot of other things we included that help with this, which I won’t go into much here to avoid spoilers, you will have to play the game and find out what they are yourself 😉

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/ca752fcb5bf80533fcfe4db83e50bb4523a07070.png[/img]

As I mentioned earlier, from a design perspective, the train’s look is inspired by the Orient express and late 1800s architecture, with lots of wooden panels and a more “upper class” feel, which makes it stylistically quite different from other levels. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/6e37d422aeee6c2b1662041b01fb88ab6af56482.png[/img]

The train has also been less affected by the events in Ground Zero compared to other areas in the game like Gamcheon, since it has mostly been dormant. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/6b63fb9cee6e5966affe39642eea9bb206ca2db3.png[/img]

On a personal note, I think my favorite aspect of this level is that the cramped space and linear design allowed us to really focus on a smaller area, which in turn led to us making a really unique area! It’s not just art related either. I think the design work as a whole on the train is really strong, where the cramped area and difficulty of kiting enemies becomes one of the level’s strong suits! 

Until next time, 
- Sixten

notes.title: Ground Zero Featuring in TPS Fest!
notes.content:
[h3]You might be looking from a third-person perspective, but that doesn’t mean you’re taking a backseat to the action 🔫

We’re excited to announce that Ground Zero will be featured in TPS Fest, a celebration of third-person shooter games from all genres![/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/19e2d29a45133e51a9f4eefc08ec28ecbf957b93.png[/img]

What do you get when you combine a gameplay loop about shooting, and a third-person perspective? Yes - you get third-person shooters, and that’s what this Fest is all about!

Like the classic survival horror games that inspired us, Ground Zero is played from the third-person perspective of the main character Seo-Yeon, an elite Korean operative who has been tasked with investigating a mysterious meteor impact site. You’ll need to take advantage of a variety of guns and other ranged weapons to defend yourself from the horrifying monstrosities that have infested your homeland following the meteor impact. 

TPS Fest starts today and ends on [b]Monday September 1st[/b], so don’t forget to wishlist Ground Zero and check out some of the other amazing discounts before the event ends!

notes.title: Dev Diary #4: Level Design in Ground Zero
notes.content:
[h3]Hello there! My name is Nathan and I’m the Lead Level Designer for Ground Zero.[/h3]

I just wanted to say up front that I'm extremely humbled and excited at the level of interest that you, the reader, and so many others have shown for our game. Thank you so much for the support, it really means a lot! In this dev diary, I wanted to give some insight into what goes on behind-the-scenes when designing and creating the levels for GZ and maybe even teach some of you something new!

[h3]A little about me.[/h3]

I’m a lifelong gamer and survival horror superfan. My gaming roots are primarily in first person shooters and I grew up playing a lot of the FPS classics like Quake, Doom, Wolfenstein, and most importantly, Half-Life 1. HL1 was my entry point into modding & level design as a kid and it singlehandedly ignited my passion and led to me pursuing it as a career. My love for survival horror came almost entirely from my dad, who I watched play countless hours of Silent Hill and Resident Evil games back then. When I played the games myself, the gameplay loop had me addicted and I loved the feeling of being scared and having to make good use of limited resources. There isn’t anything quite like it in my opinion!

[h3]How do you get started when making new maps for Ground Zero?[/h3]

As with most games, the first objective when starting a new map is to nail down the design. Some games rely heavily on the layout of the level being specifically tailored to support the game’s mechanics (for example games that incorporate parkour / movement mechanics or basically any stealth game), while other games lean more on the storytelling and pacing. GZ falls primarily in the latter category. For the most part, we can design our maps based on what we find cool and what works for specific ideas (puzzles, cutscenes, etc.) that we might have. It also means that nearly any setting or location is viable from a gameplay perspective, and this is a primary contributor to the high variety of environments seen in GZ.

Of course, there are still some cases where we design things in a very specific way. In those cases, I'll take the standard approach, which usually involves drawing a topdown and making a whiteboxed level to prototype the idea, then iterating from there through playtesting and feedback. It’s also common that I’ll write up a list of the gameplay “beats” and make a flowchart that we can use to figure out how the puzzles and other sequences will go before sitting down in the editor.

Here are a few examples of some old sketches of existing levels in the game:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/6d8dcc4de020b189463f02519660d6b348111510.png[/img][i]Original sketch of the Village map.[/i]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/7f9f0d5fbe5fd587098a31922b0d37ed48ae81c1.png[/img][i]Original sketch of the Amusement Park map.[/i]

[h3]Are there any specific games that have influenced the level design in Ground Zero?[/h3]

I’d say the  classic Resident Evils (especially RE3) and the first three Silent Hill games, but there are many inspirations and references from a handful of games (some even outside of the survival horror genre) that can be seen all over the place in GZ’s level design. Maybe you'll notice some when you play!

[h3]How do you choose how to position the cameras?[/h3]

This is quite a bit more complicated than you might think! When we first started the project, I thought of camera placement as being as simple as placing a camera in a position that you thought looked cool, and then calling it a day. I realized very quickly that there's actually somewhat of a “science” to it. GZ is a fixed-camera game, which means that the player cannot control what they see. This is in contrast to almost all other types of games, where as a level designer, you can create a scene and leave the player free to look around at their leisure and take in the world you've created.

In GZ, due to the fixed camera, we have to do it all. We have to allow you to see where you're going and what you’re doing but, at the same time, *also* show off the world and allow you to take in the environment through unique and interesting camera angles. It’s not uncommon at all that specific sections of a level are created with specific camera angles in mind, and this is easily one of the biggest differences between making levels for GZ and pretty much any other game I've ever worked on or modded for.

The best camera angles incorporate the following, in order of importance:
[olist]
[*] Clear “exit routes” that show where the player needs to move to exit the camera angle and progress forward
[*] No locations where enemies, items, or the player themself are able to move completely out of sight of the camera
[*] Objectives, items, enemies, and any other objects of importance clearly visible
[*] A clear view of the scene so that the player can fight enemies and properly gauge the playable space. To this end, we typically keep the intended gameplay space clean of debris and other obstructions to make it easy to tell where the player can and cannot move. We can also use the high contrast created by clashing colors and lights to more clearly define the walkable space as well
[*] Aesthetically pleasing visuals
[/olist]
Here’s an example of a camera angle that I feel accomplishes all of these rather well:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/1a6c87140823f86e559b353978ae5799e07eb995.gif[/img]

[h3]What’s your favorite level that you’ve worked on for Ground Zero?[/h3]

Without a doubt, it would be the top of the lighthouse that can be seen at the beginning of the game. It’s based on the real-life Yeongdo Lighthouse, and when we were considering it as a destination, I wanted to leverage it as a nice payoff to all the work the player has done.

You travel pretty far in the game, and once you finally arrive and reach the top, you get a breathtaking view of everywhere you've been up until that point, which helps tie it all together.

I've tried to incorporate these types of vistas into the game whenever I can, because they help to show off the sheer scale of the world in GZ, something which only adds to the immersion and atmosphere in my opinion.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/669591d4de69ab5a783964747a08f8ffad9d214b.png[/img]

A close contender for me would be our in-game recreation of the Bolle-gil coastal trail. In real-life, it’s a really cool oceanside walkway in the Busan region that has a very distinct red metallic look and tons of beautiful viewpoints of the coast and city.

I love the winding nature of the trail and how it snakes around the cliffs, and I’ve tried to capture that essence as much as possible in the in-game version. It’s one of the most unique areas in the game and I had a lot of fun working on it!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/9b9d81768ab61f09cd3f5e231e1fc0ebf65c3644.png[/img]

That being said, I’ve thoroughly enjoyed working on just about every part of this game, and it’s honestly so hard to boil it all down to just one or two favorites. South Korea is a beautiful country, full of amazing architecture and cool areas that have kept me more than inspired while working on the game.

Thanks for reading and I'm really excited for you all to see the rest of what we have in store!

Until next time,
- Nathan

notes.title: Dev Diary #3: An Interview with Voice Actor Evan Sabba
notes.content:
[h3]Hey! My name is Evan Sabba and I’m the voice actor behind Evan in Ground Zero, the elite operative from Canada who accompanies Seo-Yeon during her investigation of the meteor impact site in South Korea. I’m excited to do this interview to talk about my voice acting career so far and what it’s been like voicing Evan![/h3]

[b]When did you first know that you wanted to pursue a career in voice acting?[/b]

I think it was something I always wanted to do since childhood. I remember growing up on Star Wars and Battlestar Galactica, which inspired me to want to act out scenes from the shows. One day day, I found my mother’s THE PLANETS record, composed by GUSTAV HOLST (which I believe John Williams built a lot of the Star Wars music from), and would play along to it. It’s very dramatic music, so I would use it to act out scenes on my own or with my friends and we’d record them on my mother’s cassette recorder. We did whole hallway walking scenes, captain in his command chair scenes, engine room scenes, discovery scenes, and of course battle scenes! Obviously we’d make our own laser and explosion sound effects as well, to make it more realistic. So really, acting has ALWAYS been a huge part of my life.

[b]Describe what your career has been like so far, from the point when you first started voice acting to now.[/b]

This is a challenge to answer, since the truth is filled with heartache, broken dreams, missed opportunities, self loathing, self appreciation, desperation, excitement, blessings, thunderous applause, brilliant successes, tears of joy. The highs and the lows from seeing yourself on the big screen to not working for years at a stretch. You know those face masks? Comedy and Tragedy? Turns out those are pretty accurate when it comes to being an actor! It’s been a ride so far, but I wouldn’t have it any other way. It’s hard to want or imagine any other life for myself.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/268b3b135bc22615ab2377aba196015ce9bd9c3e.jpg[/img][i]Evan Sabba.[/i]

[b]What challenges do you face as a voice actor in the games industry?[/b]

We all know the big one. AI replacement. Everything is like that old game PONG right now. PONG released on November 29th 1972. Look where we are now with games. Didn’t take long to get here, right? So imagine AI Voice mapping and reproduction is PONG right NOW as of 2025. Paying artists with dignity and appreciation will go out the window when no one thinks of it as an art. 

I fear corporate directions and interests will pollute the world with data produced noise, rather than lovingly captured real human voices. A human’s voice is shaped by the performer’s whole extremely diverse life, the joy and the pain of existence. I fear AI will dehumanize concepts of art and existence.

[b]What other games have you worked on besides Ground Zero?[/b]

I had the extreme pleasure of voicing Brad Vickers in Resident Evil 3: Nemesis. Yes, I am the guy who Nemesis takes out at the RPD. He was after STARS members, and there was no escape for me. Jill got away though. She was lucky and made it out somehow. Good for her, I guess!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/efea90d0ecc0659be45ad3edd2b0f3de1233b045.png[/img]
[i]Character art of Brad Vickers from Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.
[/i]

[b]What types of games do you like to play in your free time?[/b]

I play EVERYTHING. I mean it. There are some types of games I do not play for longer stretches than others, but eventually I will at least try them. I do not have the time to finish all the games I own, which seems to be a common issue with gamers! I will at least try and see some of the artwork, design, controls, and imagination at play for however briefly I get with a game. It’s sort of like going to a gallery to see some paintings. I may spend more time looking at one painting than another, but I want to see all the paintings I can. I’m there letting the painting affect me. Let what I am looking at IN and feel what emotions and thoughts the painter wanted to create in me. That’s how I like to give time to every game I play. Be it jank, AAA, slow, fast, too fast. For me, it’s about letting the art of it all in and letting it take you away. If it doesn’t hit for me, I move on quicker.

[b]What has it been like stepping into the shoes of Evan?[/b]

Pretty easy. I am already an Evan and, as a proud member of the Order of Evans, I have to know at least half of all other Evans’ mindsets and emotions before embarking on a role with such magnitude which, I might add, only an Evan could perform. I hope that explains it. If it doesn’t (and it probably won’t, since only an ordained member of the Order of Evans could possibly understand), then the performance mainly started to take shape after some detailed discussions between myself and Ground Zero’s lead developer James over the course of two weeks. We had live sessions for recording, so there were adjustments on the fly and it was a great deal of fun. I can’t wait to see what they do with all the audio!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/0a1afafcf3ea083250bc22c61bc5ad8783f781b3.png[/img]

[b]What do you do in order to get in character before you record your lines? Are there any other characters, TV shows, games, films, etc. that you draw inspiration from when becoming Evan (the Ground Zero Evan, that is!)?[/b]

I think, once you get an idea of what you are good at, you do lean on performances that you loved growing up or just think are perfect moments to try in a scene. I think knowing myself and my range, there is always a part of Hudson balanced by Hicks from Aliens in my performance that I like to tap into.

[b]What’s been the highlight of working on Ground Zero so far?[/b]

I love working on a smaller project like this. I got to know James and what he was going for a lot better from casual discussions about his game and his passion behind wanting to create it. I am honored he asked me to voice such a fantastic character and be a part of his game. It has been a deep wish of mine to be in a game again, and to be in a game set in the same classical style as early Resident Evil games is a dream come true.

[b]Once they’ve finished the game, how do you want players to feel about Evan? What type of person is he?[/b]

I think Evan is extremely sharp but a bit of a joker. He’s very caring but brings chaos when needed. He’s also always a little hangry.

[b]If you met Evan in real life, do you think you’d get along?[/b]

Sure, but I would have to let him poke fun at me for a while.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/00abbdacb9af3496fc3d12316f54d5e5129f54ed.gif[/img]

[h3]If you’ve enjoyed this dev diary, then don’t forget to follow [b]Evan Sabba[/b] on [b][url=https://www.twitch.tv/ogbradvickers]Twitch[/url][/b], [b][url=https://x.com/EvanSabba]X/Twitter[/url][/b], and [b][url=https://bsky.app/profile/evansabba.bsky.social]Bluesky[/url][/b]![/h3]

notes.title: Dev Diary #2: Animating Seo-Yeon
notes.content:
[h3]My name is Janz. I’m the animation artist for Ground Zero and I want to talk about my process when animating Ground Zero’s main character, Seo-Yeon. [/h3]

In terms of the technical process, I first wait for the character design to be completed by the 3D artist. Then, when the model and textures are finished, I make a rig for the character. There are two rigs: one for animating with controls, drivers, and constraints; and the other one for the game, called “deform bones”. There’ll be some test movements before finishing the rigging process but, with the flow of our work, I’m able to quickly proceed to animate the idle or breathing animations. Then next will be the more complex animations such as the movement animations, pain and death animations, etc. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/48f6fa2f5188937f4b4383c3ac9a0daed40582ac.gif[/img]

When it comes to animating each character, they all have their own differences in terms of their movements, their weight, and their combat, to ensure that they all move in a unique way. Animating Seo-Yeon started with very generic movements, then lead developer James and I discussed together how she should move based on her character and what she’d be doing in the game. When animating her, I got some inspiration from the anime [i]Spy x Family[/i], but not all of her movements were inspired by the anime.

https://store.steampowered.com/app/2340130/Ground_Zero/

The challenging part when it came to animating Seo-Yeon was having to learn how to animate full body characters, because I started my career in first person shooter type animations and realised that I hadn’t learnt how to create fully body character animations properly. But James believed in me, invested in me, and encouraged me to learn and to become a fully fledged animator. The other difficulty for me was exploring Blender on my own and taking a trial-and-error approach, since not all of the answers for the animation questions I had could be found on Google. It was fun though and I’ve learned a lot this way! 

My favorite animation that I’ve done for Seo-Yeon so far is her stomp, which you can see in the clip below.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/5fc20a0092cafad9e0f2c1a04cb154c1f6fe6901.gif[/img]

notes.title: New Trailer Coming in the Future Games Show Summer Showcase!
notes.content:
[h3]Are you tired of tanning? Sick of the sunlight? Do you yearn for something a little spooky this summer?

Then we’ve got you covered!

notes.title: Dev Diary #1: Recreating Taejongdae Beach & Gamcheon Village
notes.content:
[h3]My name is Sixten. I’m one of the artists working on Ground Zero.

I want to talk about the art in the first chapters in the game, which is set largely on Taejongdae Beach and in Gamcheon Village. [/h3]

The game takes place in South Korea and we try to keep true to the real world places we base our locations on. With that being said we sometimes have to take creative liberty and change some things in order for the game to play better. When we decide on a real world location we begin the process by gathering as many references as possible from that location and try to identify what characteristics that place might have. A good example is Gamcheon village which has really colorful houses and specific landmarks that are present in the real world location and in the game. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/811e3373b738d0c22a58d50e3c153b7bd316570c.png[/img]

We usually build our levels to match the real world location as much as possible, before adding the horror elements on top. 

The challenge is always to keep a balance between realism (recreating elements from the real world locations) and creative freedom. Sometimes we have to change things around in order to ensure smooth gameplay and clear visual identity and finding that balance can sometimes be a challenge.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/ed4b8e441d916293df5d845c0f58f2c750c7c797.png[/img]

The first chapters of the game are all set in the Gamcheon area. And we do a lot of work with lighting in order to tie them together with a cohesive color palette. 

My personal favorite area in the first chapters of the game is Gamcheon village. It is one of the first areas we worked on as a team and I feel immense pride seeing it all together as someone who worked on the project way back when the game was just an empty world. We’ve put in a lot of effort into making the village represent the real world location by making a lot of assets of objects that can be found in real world locations such as the arch and the fish mural.

https://store.steampowered.com/app/2340130/Ground_Zero/

Let us know in the comments 💬[/h3]

notes.title: Ground Zero Supports the Horror Game Awards 2024
notes.content:
[h3]Get ready to scream…

With excitement, because the Horror Game Awards 2024 has begun!

You can follow the link [url=https://youtu.be/VxJEQHK7YfI][b]here[/b][/url] to watch the awards show live right now.[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44188915/9329bc54034aff21e0b612915222787e3631457a.png[/img]

The Horror Game Awards were started in 2022 by Phil Dickens and Will Penkeyman. After seeing that horror games weren’t getting recognition in other award shows at a time when the genre was seeing a resurgence in both popularity and quality, they decided to create an awards show entirely dedicated to the spookiest in class.

We’re honoured that Ground Zero was selected to be an official participant in the event!

In Ground Zero, you’ll take on the role of Seo-Yeon, an elite Korean operative who has been tasked with investigating the meteor impact site in her homeland. Back up by her Canadian counterpart Evan, Seo-Yeon must make her way through the post-apocalyptic landscape, gather biological data on the mutated creatures that inhabit it, and piece together the mystery behind this anomalous event.  

Our retro horror style was inspired by all of the incredible horror games that we’ve played throughout the years, so it’s wonderful to see games in the horror genre start to get the recognition they deserve and be given their own awards show. We hope that you’ll join us in supporting the awards show this year! Who knows, maybe next year you’ll even have the chance to vote for Ground Zero in the Horror Game Awards 2025?
